title: The Voice on the Lost Phone

pages.text: The phone was on the ground beside the bench near the estate gate. It was not cracked. It was not wet. It had simply been put down and forgotten, or dropped and not noticed. Nosa picked it up and looked around. Nobody seemed to be missing a phone. He carried it to the shade under the mango tree and sat down to think.

image.note: Illustration: Nosa crouching beside a bench near a gate, holding up a phone, looking around the empty estate road

pages.text: The screen lit up. Not because anyone was calling. Because a voice note notification appeared. A voice note addressed to nobody. Already open. Already playing.
'Hello? I fell. I am on the path behind the wall near the small generator house. I can't get up. Can someone come? I am scared.' A child's voice. Young. Trying not to cry.
Nosa sat very still for a moment. Then he listened again to make sure he had heard correctly. He had. He looked at the phone. The screen said the voice note had been sent forty-seven minutes ago.

Nosa turned the phone over in his hands. It was an ordinary phone, the sort half the estate carried, in a blue case worn pale at the corners. He pressed the side button again and the voice note played again, the same small frightened voice, the same words. He looked at the time on the lock screen and did the sum in his head. Forty-seven minutes. Whoever had recorded it had been waiting forty-seven minutes, and no one had come.

That was the part Nosa could not walk away from. A voice note only mattered if someone heard it, and this one had been sent to a phone that was lying, forgotten, in the grass by the gate. The person who should have heard it never had. Nosa was not sure the child on the recording was still where she said she was. He was not sure of anything. But he was sure that doing nothing was no longer a thing he was allowed to do.

Titi arrived at the mango tree carrying a snack she immediately forgot about when Nosa played the voice note to her. She listened twice, which was one more time than Nosa had thought necessary. Then she produced a small notebook from her school bag and began writing.

image.note: Illustration: Titi at the mango tree, notebook open, pen moving fast, Nosa watching her

pages.text: 'Step one,' Titi said, 'find out who this phone belongs to. Step two, find out who sent the voice note. Step three, establish that the child is safe. Step four, return the phone to its owner with a full account of what happened so they understand why it took this long.' She looked up. 'Are you writing this down?' 'I don't have a notebook,' Nosa said. 'Why do you not have a notebook?' 'Because I wasn't expecting to need one,' Nosa said.

Ini had appeared while they were talking, as Ini often did. 'The phone is locked,' she said. She had been looking at it while they discussed the plan. 'We can't call anyone from it. We can't look at the contacts. We can only see the lock screen.' She handed it back to Nosa. 'But the lock screen shows the emergency call button.'
Titi looked at Ini. 'You could have said that before I wrote step one.' 'You seemed to be enjoying writing step one,' Ini said.

Titi read the four steps aloud once more, then underlined step one twice, which was her way of taking a thing seriously. She was the kind of person who believed that any problem could be beaten if it was broken into small enough pieces and the pieces were tackled in order. It was a good quality, mostly. It occasionally meant she was still numbering the steps of a plan when the situation had already moved three steps ahead of her.

Ini did not make plans. Ini watched. She had picked the phone up while Titi wrote, turned it over, tried the buttons, and put it down again, and in doing so had learned the one fact that mattered most: the phone was locked, and everything Titi's plan depended on, the contacts, the messages, the owner's name, was sealed behind that lock. She waited for a gap in Titi's numbering, and then, gently, she said so.

Calling the emergency number on the locked phone connected them to a calm security officer who explained that she could not send assistance based on a voice note from an unknown child about an unconfirmed location unless there was a specific address. She was helpful and clear and entirely unable to help them. Remigius was not at the gate; the guardhouse was empty. There were no adults immediately available on the estate road. Titi put a line through step one.

Titi moved to step three, which was easier than step one or step two. They went to the path behind the wall near the small generator house, which was on the west side of the estate and took four minutes to reach at a fast walk.

image.note: Illustration: Nosa, Titi and Ini walking quickly along an estate path, generator house visible in the background

pages.text: A girl of about seven was sitting on the ground near a tree root that had lifted the path surface into a small ridge. She had a dirty knee and had been crying recently but had stopped. She looked up at them with the expression of someone who has decided that being found is probably better than not being found.

'I tripped,' she said. 'I couldn't get up because my ankle hurt. It's better now. I sent a voice note to my sister's phone. She has it.' 'Your sister's phone is here,' Nosa said, and held it up. The girl looked at it with great interest. 'She will be very upset,' she said, not sounding entirely sorry about this.

The girl's name was Kemi Junior, which was what her family called her to distinguish her from an aunt named Kemi. She was not, she explained, supposed to be on the path by herself. She was supposed to be at her cousin's flat. She had made a detour to look at the generator house, which she found interesting. The tree root had not been her friend.

image.note: Illustration: Kemi Junior sitting up against the wall explaining herself to three older children

pages.text: Her sister arrived at a run six minutes later, having noticed the phone was gone, having retraced her steps to the bench, and having found only the phone absent and three older children missing from the estate. The sister's name was Kachi, she was eleven, and she appeared more relieved than angry, though she was working hard to maintain a balance of both.

Kachi looked at her phone. She looked at the voice note. She looked at her sister. 'You couldn't stand up?' 'My ankle hurt,' Kemi Junior said. 'It doesn't hurt now.' 'That's because you've been sitting for fifty minutes.' 'I was waiting,' Kemi Junior said with great dignity.

Titi showed Kachi her notebook. 'We worked through a four-step plan,' she said. Kachi read it. 'Step one is crossed out,' she said. 'We pivoted to step three,' Titi said, as though this were entirely normal. Ini said nothing, which meant she agreed.

They walked back to the main estate road together. Kemi Junior limped slightly, but briskly, and showed them a crack in the generator house wall that she said made a humming sound in a certain kind of weather. 'You can tell the electricity is on the other side,' she said, with great authority. Nobody disputed this. Some things did not need testing to be believed. Nosa stayed longer than the others thought necessary, listening from a respectful distance, which was apparently the right distance for electricity.
